stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 6.7 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 295 K and 1.01 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 38.0 mL of 0.14 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 3 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.13 M NaOH.
2.5 g of $$\ce{NH4NO3}$$ dissolves in 135 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 9.7 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Mg electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$$ and a Cu electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Cu^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Mg^{2+} + 2e- -> Mg}$$ E° = -2.37 V; $$\ce{Cu^{2+} + 2e- -> Cu}$$ E° = 0.34 V.
The photoelectron spectra of Mg (Z = 12) and Al (Z = 13) are compared.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.1 M solution of $$\ce{NaOH}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 1 × 0.1 M; pH = 14 − pOH.
That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 27.2 g. The actual yield is 24.8 g. What is the percent yield?
How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{HCN}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: At equilibrium, which statement is true?

options.text: Forward and reverse reaction rates are equal
Reactant and product concentrations are equal
options.why: They are constant, not necessarily equal.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 41 min. Starting at 17.1 M, what is the concentration after 205 min?

options.why: Each half-life halves the concentration; it is not divided by 2n.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 38.4 g. The actual yield is 37.6 g. What is the percent yield?
Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.2).

questions.stem: Which process has a negative ΔS?
What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 274 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.1 mol N₂, 0.2 mol O₂ and 0.6 mol Ar at a total pressure of 4.9 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of H in $$\ce{C3H8}$$?

options.why: Use masses, not numbers of atoms.
That is the percent of the other elements.
There are 8 atoms of H in the formula.

questions.stem: What is the pressure of 2.07 mol of gas in a 40 L container at 328 K?

options.why: With L and atm, use R = 0.08206.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 2.8. A mixture has [A] = 0.3 M, [B] = 0.4 M and [C] = 0.3 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 2.5
It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.75
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.75
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.75, which is less than K.

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K

questions.stem: Which best explains why the atomic radius of Cl is smaller than that of Na?

options.why: They are in the same period.

options.text: Cl has more protons with similar shielding, so its valence electrons are pulled closer
options.why: Correct. Greater effective nuclear charge across a period.

questions.explanation: Greater effective nuclear charge across a period.

questions.stem: Which is a physical change?

options.why: Correct. Only intermolecular forces are overcome.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 32. What is K for the reaction multiplied by ½?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest acid?

options.why: Correct. More oxygen atoms stabilize the conjugate base.

questions.explanation: More oxygen atoms stabilize the conjugate base.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 10.4. In a solution at pH 7.9, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: Why does increasing temperature increase reaction rate?

options.text: A larger fraction of collisions have energy at or above the activation energy

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 16. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.

questions.stem: Steel is harder than pure iron because:

options.text: Small carbon atoms in the gaps (interstitial alloy) hinder layers of iron atoms from sliding
Carbon replaces iron atoms of the same size

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.18 mol of solute in enough water to make 346 mL of solution?
Samples of $$\ce{Ar}$$, $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: Ar 40, Cl2 70.9, N2 28, H2 2.02.

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of aluminum (Al, Z = 13)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 13 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{O2}$$, $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: O2 32, He 4, N2 28, CO2 44.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 453 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: What is the hybridization of the central atom in $$\ce{H2O}$$?

options.why: Count electron domains, including lone pairs.
Correct. Hybridization matches the number of electron domains: 2 sp, 3 sp², 4 sp³.
Count electron domains, including lone pairs.
Count electron domains, including lone pairs.

questions.explanation: H2O has 4 electron domains on the central atom.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4; doubling [B] multiplies it by 2.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×4, so order 2 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×2, so order 1 in B.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ is consumed at 0.06 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NH3}$$ form?

options.why: Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 2/3.
Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 113 kJ/mol, the transition state at 238 kJ/mol and the products at 95 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the forward reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 125, ΔH = -18, reverse Ea = 143 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: 77 g of water at 52 °C is mixed with 48 g of water at 15 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.
Pair each mass with its own temperature.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{NaF}$$ or $$\ce{BaO}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{NaF}$$, because its ions have larger charges
They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{NaF}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: $$\ce{BaO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

questions.explanation: BaO has ion charges 2 and 2; NaF has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 465 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of S in $$\ce{SO2}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: A 37.3 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 41 mL of 0.171 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$, $$\ce{Cl2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.

questions.explanation: Molar masses: He 4, O2 32, Ar 40, Cl2 70.9.

questions.stem: Which substance is most soluble in hexane (C₆H₁₄)?

options.why: Ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.9 mol N₂, 0.4 mol O₂ and 0.2 mol Ar at a total pressure of 4.2 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 0.433 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 197 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
Why is the enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?

options.text: Vaporization separates molecules completely, overcoming all intermolecular forces

questions.stem: 28 mL of 0.27 M weak acid HA is titrated with 0.29 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH reaches the equivalence point?

options.why: Correct. Moles of base = moles of acid.

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 5 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 1. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}\,3p^{1}$$, which has 13 electrons.

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = 63 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -111 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 294 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Convert ΔS from J to kJ.
Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{Mg(OH)2}$$ is 5.6 \times 10^{-12}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
A compound (ethane) is 79.9% C, 20.1% H by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to CH3; the molecular formula is C2H6.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4; doubling [B] multiplies it by 1.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×4, so order 2 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×1, so order 0 in B.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.12 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 4.74) and 0.29 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
How can an unfavorable reaction (ΔG positive) be made to occur?

options.text: By coupling it to a favorable reaction so the total ΔG is negative

questions.stem: For the galvanic cell made from these half-cells, what is ΔG°? (F = 96,485 C/mol)

options.why: Correct. ΔG° = −nFE° with n = 6 electrons transferred and E° = 0.9 V.
ΔG° is negative for a positive E°.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.34 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 7.21) and 0.09 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is 7 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = -2.83; K = 0.0593. Positive ΔG°: K less than 1.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O(l)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).
Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.5 M solution of hydrofluoric acid (Ka = 6.8 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 4.2) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 72.3 mL. What is the pH after 36.2 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.
That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.047 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 125 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature falls by 12.2 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).
Divide by the moles of reactant.
Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 6370 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{H2 + F2 -> 2HF}$$.

options.why: Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 605, 1150, 10350, 15215 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Correct. The large jump comes after removing 2 electrons, so it has 2 valence electrons.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1.4 M and [I₂] = 1.7 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 1.54 M. What is K?
For $$\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O}$$, 84 g of $$\ce{CH4}$$ reacts with 19 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{CO2}$$ can form?

options.why: Not all of both reactants reacts.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Correct. O2 is the limiting reactant.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -396 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = 113 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and adding reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 1.428 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in ln[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: X → Y + Z. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Mg²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.01 M I⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Would lowering the pH significantly change the solubility? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: No: I⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so H⁺ does not remove it.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of Al.
Explain why the 1s peak of Al has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of Mg.

rubric.criterion: Al has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: Al has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: Mg: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
